source_text:
CHAPTER LVIII.
A Final Understanding.


Tito soon returned from Siena, but almost immediately set out on
another journey, from which he did not return till the seventeenth of
August. Nearly a fortnight had passed since the arrest of the accused,
and still they were in prison, still their fate was uncertain. Romola
had felt during this interval as if all cares were suspended for her,
other than watching the fluctuating probabilities concerning that fate.
Sometimes they seemed strongly in favour of the prisoners; for the
chances of effective interest on their behalf were heightened by delay,
and an indefinite prospect of delay was opened by the reluctance of all
persons in authority to incur the odium attendant on any decision. On
the one side there was a loud cry that the Republic was in danger, and
that lenity to the prisoners would be the signal of attack for all its
enemies; on the other, there was a certainty that a sentence of death
and confiscation of property passed on five citizens of distinguished
name, would entail the rancorous hatred of their relatives on all who
were conspicuously instrumental to such a sentence.

The final judgment properly lay with the Eight, who presided over the
administration of criminal justice; and the sentence depended on a
majority of six votes. But the Eight shrank from their onerous
responsibility, and asked in this exceptional case to have it shared by
the Signoria (or the Gonfaloniere and the eight Priors). The Signoria
in its turn shrugged its shoulders, and proposed the appeal to the
Great Council. For, according to a law passed by the earnest persuasion
of Savonarola nearly three years before, whenever a citizen was
condemned to death by the fatal six votes (called the _set fave_ or
_six beans_, beans being in more senses than one the political pulse of
Florence), he had the right of appealing from that sentence to the
Great Council.

But in this stage of the business, the friends of the accused resisted
the appeal, determined chiefly by the wish to gain delay; and, in fact,
strict legality required that sentence should have been passed prior to
the appeal. Their resistance prevailed, and a middle course was taken;
the sentence was referred to a large assembly convened on the
seventeenth, consisting of all the higher magistracies, the smaller
council or Senate of Eighty, and a select number of citizens.

On this day Romola, with anxiety heightened by the possibility that
before its close her godfather’s fate might be decided, had obtained
leave to see him for the second time, but only in the presence of
witnesses. She had returned to the Via de’ Bardi in company with her
cousin Brigida, still ignorant whether the council had come to any
decisive issue; and Monna Brigida had gone out again to await the
momentous news at the house of a friend belonging to one of the
magistracies, that she might bring back authentic tidings as soon as
they were to be had.

Romola had sunk on the first seat in the bright saloon, too much
agitated, too sick at heart, to care about her place, or be conscious
of discordance in the objects that surrounded her. She sat with her
back to the door, resting her head on her hands. It seemed a long while
since Monna Brigida had gone, and Romola was expecting her return. But
when the door opened she knew it was not Monna Brigida who entered.

Since she had parted from Tito on that memorable night, she had had no
external proof to warrant her belief that he had won his safety by
treachery; on the contrary, she had had evidence that he was still
trusted by the Mediceans, and was believed by them to be accomplishing
certain errands of theirs in Romagna, under cover of fulfilling a
commission of the government. For the obscurity in which the evidence
concerning the conspirators was shrouded allowed it to be understood
that Tito had escaped any implication.

But Romola’s suspicion was not to be dissipated: her horror of his
conduct towards Baldassarre projected itself over every conception of
his acts; it was as if she had seen him committing a murder, and had
had a diseased impression ever after that his hands were covered with
fresh blood.

As she heard his step on the stone floor, a chill shudder passed
through her; she could not turn round, she could not rise to give any
greeting. He did not speak, but after an instant’s pause took a seat on
the other side of the table just opposite to her. Then she raised her
eyes and looked at him; but she was mute. He did not show any
irritation, but said, coolly—

“This meeting corresponds with our parting, Romola. But I understand
that it is a moment of terrible suspense. I am come, however, if you
will listen to me, to bring you the relief of hope.”

She started, and altered her position, but looked at him dubiously.

“It will not be unwelcome to you to hear—even though it is I who tell
it—that the council is prorogued till the twenty-first. The Eight have
been frightened at last into passing a sentence of condemnation, but
the demand has now been made on behalf of the condemned for the Appeal
to the Great Council.”

Romola’s face lost its dubious expression; she asked eagerly—

“And when is it to be made?”

“It has not yet been granted; but it _may_ be granted. The Special
Council is to meet again on the twenty-first to deliberate whether the
Appeal shall be allowed or not. In the meantime there is an interval of
three days, in which chances may occur in favour of the prisoners—in
which interest may be used on their behalf.”

Romola started from her seat. The colour had risen to her face like a
visible thought, and her hands trembled. In that moment her feeling
towards Tito was forgotten.

“Possibly,” said Tito, also rising, “your own intention may have
anticipated what I was going to say. You are thinking of the Frate.”

“I am,” said Romola, looking at him with surprise. “Has he done
anything? Is there anything to tell me?”

“Only this. It was Messer Francesco Valori’s bitterness and violence
which chiefly determined the course of things in the council to-day.
Half the men who gave in their opinion against the prisoners were
frightened into it, and there are numerous friends of Fra Girolamo both
in this Special Council and out of it who are strongly opposed to the
sentence of death—Piero Guicciardini, for example, who is one member of
the Signoria that made the stoutest resistance; and there is Giovan
Battista Ridolfi, who, Piagnone as he is, will not lightly forgive the
death of his brother Niccolò.”

“But how can the Appeal be denied,” said Romola, indignantly, “when it
is the law—when it was one of the chief glories of the popular
government to have passed the law?”

“They call this an exceptional case. Of course there are ingenious
arguments, but there is much more of loud bluster about the danger of
the Republic. But, you see, no opposition could prevent the assembly
from being prorogued, and a certain powerful influence rightly applied
during the next three days might determine the wavering courage of
those who desire that the Appeal should be granted, and might even give
a check to the headlong enmity of Francesco Valori. It happens to have
come to my knowledge that the Frate has so far interfered as to send a
message to him in favour of Lorenzo Tornabuoni. I know you can
sometimes have access to the Frate: it might at all events be worth
while to use your privilege now.”

“It is true,” said Romola, with an air of abstraction. “I cannot
believe that the Frate would approve denying the Appeal.”

“I heard it said by more than one person in the court of the Palazzo,
before I came away, that it would be to the everlasting discredit of
Fra Girolamo if he allowed a government which is almost entirely made
up of his party, to deny the Appeal, without entering his protest, when
he has been boasting in his books and sermons that it was he who got
the law passed.[1] But between ourselves, with all respect for your
Frate’s ability, my Romola, he has got into the practice of preaching
that form of human sacrifices called killing tyrants and wicked
malcontents, which some of his followers are likely to think
inconsistent with lenity in the present case.”

 [1] The most recent, and in some respects the best, biographer of
 Savonarola, Signor Villari, endeavours to show that the Law of Appeal
 ultimately enacted, being wider than the law originally contemplated
 by Savonarola, was a source of bitter annoyance to him, as a
 contrivance of the aristocratic party for attaching to the measures of
 the popular government the injurious results of licence. But in taking
 this view the estimable biographer lost sight of the fact that, not
 only in his sermons, but in a deliberately prepared book (the
 _Compendium Revelationum_) written long after the Appeal had become
 law, Savonarola enumerates among the benefits secured to Florence,
 “_the Appeal from the Six Votes, advocated by me, for the greater
 security of the citizens_.”


“I know, I know,” said Romola, with a look and tone of pain. “But he is
driven into those excesses of speech. It used to be different. I _will_
ask for an interview. I cannot rest without it. I trust in the
greatness of his heart.”

She was not looking at Tito; her eyes were bent with a vague gaze
towards the ground, and she had no distinct consciousness that the
words she heard came from her husband.

“Better lose no time, then,” said Tito, with unmixed suavity, moving
his cap round in his hands as if he were about to put it on and depart.
“And now, Romola, you will perhaps be able to see, in spite of
prejudice, that my wishes go with yours in this matter. You will not
regard the misfortune of my safety as an offence.”

Something like an electric shock passed through Romola: it was the full
consciousness of her husband’s presence returning to her. She looked at
him without speaking.

“At least,” he added, in a slightly harder tone, “you will endeavour to
base our intercourse on some other reasonings than that because an evil
deed is possible, _I_ have done it. Am I alone to be beyond the pale of
your extensive charity?”

The feeling which had been driven back from Romola’s lips a fortnight
before rose again with the gathered force of a tidal wave. She spoke
with a decision which told him that she was careless of consequences.

“It is too late, Tito. There is no killing the suspicion that deceit
has once begotten. And now I know everything. I know who that old man
was: he was your father, to whom you owe everything—to whom you owe
more than if you had been his own child. By the side of that, it is a
small thing that you broke my trust and my father’s. As long as you
deny the truth about that old man, there is a horror rising between us:
the law that should make us one can never be obeyed. I too am a human
being. I have a soul of my own that abhors your actions. Our union is a
pretence—as if a perpetual lie could be a sacred marriage.”

Tito did not answer immediately. When he did speak it was with a
calculated caution, that was stimulated by alarm.

“And you mean to carry out that independence by quitting me, I
presume?”

“I desire to quit you,” said Romola, impetuously.

“And supposing I do not submit to part with what the law gives me some
security for retaining? You will then, of course, proclaim your reasons
in the ear of all Florence. You will bring forward your mad assassin,
who is doubtless ready to obey your call, and you will tell the world
that you believe his testimony because he is so rational as to desire
to assassinate me. You will first inform the Signoria that I am a
Medicean conspirator, and then you will inform the Mediceans that I
have betrayed them, and in both cases you will offer the excellent
proof that you believe me capable in general of everything bad. It will
certainly be a striking position for a wife to adopt. And if, on such
evidence, you succeed in holding me up to infamy, you will have
surpassed all the heroines of the Greek drama.”

He paused a moment, but she stood mute. He went on with the sense of
mastery.

“I believe you have no other grievance against me—except that I have
failed in fulfilling some lofty indefinite conditions on which you gave
me your wifely affection, so that, by withdrawing it, you have
gradually reduced me to the careful supply of your wants as a fair
Piagnone of high condition and liberal charities. I think your success
in gibbeting me is not certain. But doubtless you would begin by
winning the ear of Messer Bernardo del Nero?”

“Why do I speak of anything?” cried Romola, in anguish, sinking on her
chair again. “It is hateful in me to be thinking of myself.”

She did not notice when Tito left the room, or know how long it was
before the door opened to admit Monna Brigida. But in that instant she
started up and said—

“Cousin, we must go to San Marco directly. I must see my confessor, Fra
Salvestro.”

Tito had scarcely returned to Florence from Siena before he set out on a second urgent journey, and did not come back until the seventeenth of August. Nearly a fortnight had dragged past since the arrest of the five prominent citizens accused of plotting to restore the Medici, and still they languished in the city dungeons, their fates hanging entirely unwritten, no verdict handed down to end the limbo that stretched thin the nerves of every partisan in Florence.

For Romola, those two weeks had blotted out every other care, her whole life narrowing down to watching the ebb and flow of odds that might save her godfather, Bernardo del Nero, and the other imprisoned men. At times, hope seemed almost tangible: the long delay worked in their favour, letting influential allies quietly marshal support for leniency, as every official tasked with judging the case shrank from the odium of making a final call. One faction roared that the Republic would be fatally endangered by any mercy to the plotters, that to spare them was to invite every exiled Medicean ally to march on the city gates. The other side knew full well that to sentence five men of such ancient, distinguished Florentine lineages to death and confiscation would breed generations of bitter, vengeful relatives who would never rest until every judge who signed the warrant had paid for it.

The official responsibility for criminal judgements rested with the Eight, the magistracy that oversaw Florence’s justice system, and a sentence of death required a majority of six votes – the famous sei fave, or “six beans”, named for the black and white dried beans citizens used to cast their secret votes, a small, absurd marker of the republic’s parsimonious approach to political representation. But the Eight dared not bear the weight alone, and begged the Signoria – the ruling Gonfaloniere and his eight Priors – to share the burden. The Signoria in turn shrugged off the onus, proposing instead that the accused be allowed to appeal to the Great Council, per the law Savonarola had pushed through to wide acclaim nearly three years prior.

The friends of the prisoners resisted that appeal, though, determined to drag out the delay as long as possible – and strict legal precedent did say an appeal could only be filed after a formal sentence had already been passed. Their resistance won out, and a compromise was struck: the verdict would be decided by a special, broad assembly convened that very seventeenth of August, made up of all the highest magistrates, the eighty-member Senate, and a select body of leading citizens.

That same day, Romola, her anxiety spiking at the thought her godfather’s fate might be decided before sundown, had secured permission for a second, closely supervised visit to his cell, with two guards posted within earshot the whole time. She had walked back to the Via de’ Bardi house with her cousin Monna Brigida, still entirely in the dark about what the special council had voted to do. Monna Brigida had immediately hurried off again to wait for news at the home of a relative who sat on one of the magistracies, determined to bring back the first authentic, unrumoured account of the outcome.

Romola dropped onto the first bench she spotted in the bright, frescoed saloon, too shaken, too sick at heart to care about decorum or notice the fine statues and tapestries around her. She sat with her back to the door, her head resting in her hands, waiting. It felt like an hour had passed since Brigida left, so when the door creaked open, she did not even lift her head – until the step on the stone floor told her at once this was not her cousin.

Since that terrible night she had turned Tito out of her rooms, she had held no concrete, provable evidence that he had bought his own safety by betraying his old father Baldassarre, or the secrets of the conspiracy, to the Signoria. To the contrary, all she could see was evidence that the exiled Mediceans still trusted him, believed he was running their secret errands across Romagna while posing as an agent of the Florentine republic. No official had ever named him as a conspirator, the evidence against the plotters was murky enough to leave his name entirely clear. But Romola’s suspicion would not budge: the horror of what she had seen him do to the old man blotted out every other fact about him, as if she had watched him commit a murder and could never shake the sick, certain impression his hands were still sticky with fresh blood.

A cold shudder ran down her spine as his step crossed the threshold. She could not turn, could not stand to greet him. He said nothing at first, pausing only a moment before taking a seat across the table, directly facing her. Then she lifted her eyes to meet his, still completely silent. He showed no irritation, his voice even and calm.
“This meeting mirrors our parting, Romola. But I know full well you are living through a moment of terrible, gnawing suspense. I have come, if you will listen, to bring you the relief of real hope.”

She started, shifting her weight, staring at him with open, distrustful doubt.
“The council has voted to prorogue, to delay any final verdict, until the twenty-first. The Eight were finally bullied into issuing a formal sentence of condemnation, but a formal demand has now been filed on behalf of the five prisoners to allow them to appeal to the Great Council.”

Romola’s face softened, the doubt melting away. She leaned forward, eager. “When will that appeal be heard?”
“It has not been granted yet. But it could be. The special council will meet again on the twenty-first to vote on whether to allow the appeal at all. That gives three full days, a window where favour can be called in, influence can be brought to bear, and odds can shift sharply in the prisoners’ favour.”

Romola sprang to her feet, colour flooding her cheeks, her hands trembling. In that rush of hope, all her loathing for Tito vanished for a heartbeat.
“No doubt you have already thought of what I was about to suggest,” Tito said, standing as well. “You are thinking of the Frate.”
“I am,” Romola said, surprised. “Has he acted already? Is there news of him?”
“Only this: it was Messer Francesco Valori’s rabid, violent anger that pushed most of the council to vote for condemnation today. Half the men who sided with the death sentence did it out of fear, not conviction. There are dozens of Fra Girolamo’s followers in that special council and out of it who are dead set against putting five prominent citizens to death – Piero Guicciardini, for example, who was one of the Signoria’s most vocal resisters of the sentence, and Giovan Battista Ridolfi, a devout Piagnone who will not easily forgive the death of his own brother Niccolò.”
“But how can they possibly deny the appeal?” Romola demanded, indignant. “It is the law! One of the proudest achievements of this very popular government, won by the Frate’s own preaching.”
“They claim this is an exceptional case, full of loud bluster about the Republic being on the brink of destruction. No amount of argument could stop them voting to adjourn, though. A single, powerful, well-placed influence used over these next three days could stiffen the spines of all the waverers who want to grant the appeal, and rein in Valori’s headlong hatred. I heard myself that the Frate has already sent a message to Valori to plead for mercy for Lorenzo Tornabuoni. You are the only lay person with regular, open access to the Frate. It would be more than worth your while to go to him now.”
“You are right,” Romola said, her eyes distant, lost in thought. “I cannot believe the Frate would ever stand by and let that law he fought so hard for be overturned.”
“I heard half the crowd in the Palazzo courtyard saying before I left that it would bring eternal shame on Fra Girolamo if he let a government made up almost entirely of his own followers deny that appeal, without lifting a single protest – after spending years boasting in his sermons and his books that he was the one who won that law for Florence.” Tito paused, his tone silkily smooth. “Though between us, for all your Frate’s gifts, he has fallen into the habit of preaching that violent sort of ‘human sacrifice’ that calls for killing tyrants and dissidents, and some of his followers are now wondering how to square that with showing mercy to these five men today.”

Romola winced, her face tight with pain. “I know. I know. He is driven to those excesses of speech, it was not always so. I will ask for an audience at once. I cannot rest until I speak to him. I trust the greatness of his heart.” She was not looking at Tito now, her gaze fixed on the floor, barely even registering that he was the one speaking to her.
“Then do not waste a moment,” Tito said, picking up his cap and twisting it in his hands, making as if to leave. “And now, Romola, I hope that in spite of all your prejudice against me, you can see that my own wishes are aligned with yours here. You will not hold the mere fact that I escaped implication in the conspiracy, that I kept my life, against me as an unforgivable crime.”

A jolt ran through Romola, sharp as an electric shock, dragging her back to full, sharp awareness of the man standing before her. She stared at him, silent.
“At the very least,” he added, his tone hardening a little, “you could treat our intercourse as something more than a test where if an evil deed is possible for a man, he must have done it. Am I the only person in the whole city you cannot extend your famous charity to?”

All the pain and resentment she had held back for a fortnight surged up in her, rising like a high tide that would not be dammed. She spoke with unflinching decision, unconcerned for any consequences.
“It is too late, Tito. A lie once told, a suspicion once planted, can never be killed. And I know everything now. I know who that old man was. He was your father. The man who raised you, who gave you everything, who risked his life for you more than once. Next to the horror of what you did to him, the fact that you broke my trust, and betrayed my father’s memory, is a small thing. As long as you lie about him, deny the truth of what you did, there is a chasm of loathing between us that can never be crossed. We are both human beings. I have a soul of my own, and it recoils from every action you take. Our marriage is nothing but a pretence. A perpetual lie can never be a sacred union.”

Tito did not reply at once, calculating, already spiked with alarm. When he spoke, his tone was carefully measured, cold and deliberate.
“And you intend to act on that independence by leaving me, I presume?”
“I do,” Romola said, sharp and impetuous.
“And what if I refuse to let you go?” Tito said, his tone sharpening with quiet menace. “The law gives me every right to keep my wife at my side. Will you run through every street in Florence screaming your story? Drag that mad, would-be assassin old man out of the gutters to prove your point, who everyone knows will do anything you tell him to get his revenge on me? Will you run first to the Signoria and tell them I am a secret Medicean conspirator, then run to the exiled Mediceans and tell them I betrayed their secrets? What proof do you have? Only your own word, that you are so certain I am capable of every evil imaginable. What a position that would be for a respected noble Florentine wife! If you did somehow manage to drag my name through the mud, you would be the most famous wronged heroine the Greek stage ever saw.” He paused, watching her stand mute, sensing he had the upper hand. “I do not believe you have any other grievance against me. Only that I failed to live up to some lofty, vague ideal of a husband you set for me, so you withdrew your affection, and left me to carefully tend to your public reputation as a pious, charitable leading Piagnone lady. You will find you cannot make the city believe your story. But no doubt you would start by running to your beloved godfather Bernardo del Nero with your wild tales, would you not?”

“Why am I even wasting breath talking about myself?” Romola cried out in anguish, sinking back onto her chair. It felt loathsome, selfish, to waste a single second fighting over their broken marriage when five men’s lives hung in the balance.

She did not notice when Tito slipped silently out of the room. She had no idea how long she sat there, lost in her own thoughts, until the door creaked open and Monna Brigida stepped over the threshold. Romola sprang to her feet at once.
“Cousin. We must go to San Marco this very instant. I have to see my confessor, Fra Salvestro – and the Frate.”
